name: Emeka Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Emeka. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and anything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mr Whitlock at Greyfield, about six hundred ewes and some oats and hay on the better ground. Winter days, I'm out at seven with the quad and a trailer of feed, checking the flock, then fencing, mending walls, and whatever Mr Whitlock has written on the board in the kitchen. He's seventy and still out every day. I've been with him two years, and I'm still slow with the dog, she listens to him and mostly ignores me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's honest work, and you can see what you've done at the end of the day. Mr Whitlock taught me most of what I know, like an apprentice in the old way. Sunday I'm at chapel, and Grace and I are getting married there next August, so I'm saving every penny I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time, and ask the same few questions. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. The people who sell these things always promise the earth. I'd say it after chapel, or to Mr Whitlock over tea, not online, I don't really go on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad. I've never used one of these AI programs and I don't think I'd trust what it said. I'd rather learn from a man who's been doing it fifty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep saving for the wedding and a deposit on a cottage. We've got about four months of living money put by, plus the wedding fund. Maybe I'd ask Mr Whitlock to teach me shearing properly this summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chapel in the morning, then the village hall, with Grace's mum doing the food. About eighty people. Grace wants fairy lights, I want it to be paid for. We'll find the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather learn from a man who's done it fifty years. Has Mr Whitlock ever been wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty of times, and he says so. That's the difference. He once lost twenty lambs in a late snow because he'd turned them out early, and he still talks about it as a lesson. I don't know if a computer ever says sorry.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people selling these things always promise the earth. I'd say it after chapel or over tea with my boss, not online.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad, since I've never used AI and wouldn't trust it. I'd rather learn from someone who's farmed for fifty years.
S0.do: Keeps working on the sheep farm and saving for next August's wedding and a cottage deposit, on top of about four months of living money. Asks his boss to teach him shearing properly this summer.
S0.quote: I don't know if a computer ever says sorry.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka's world is organised around chapel, his wedding and an old-style apprenticeship under his seventy-year-old boss. His distrust of AI is moral as much as practical: he values a teacher who admits mistakes. Saving is his main plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be free to get on with it, and those who lose out should be helped by their families and communities first. I don't want the government running farms. I'd say that at the young farmers' club if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't think Mr Whitlock will buy a robot. He still writes the lambing records in a book. But he's seventy, and when he stops, I don't know who takes Greyfield on. That's the real question for me, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and work harder, so I'm worth keeping whatever happens. I'd put a bit more away, maybe an extra twenty a week. I wouldn't do a computer course, I don't think, unless Mr Whitlock asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Sheep on a hill are a hard thing for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might take Greyfield on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His son lives in the city and doesn't want it. Maybe it gets sold to a bigger neighbour, or to one of these investment companies. I've prayed about it, honestly. I'd like to be the one, but I'd need money I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd work harder rather than learn the new kit. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. But it's what I know how to do. My father always said the man who shows up early is never the first to go. I hope he was right.

S1.say: I'd say people should be free to get on with it, and those who lose out should be helped by family and community first, not the government running farms.
S1.think: My boss won't buy a robot, but he's seventy, and who takes the farm on when he stops matters more to me than the machines.
S1.do: Carries on and works harder to be worth keeping, adding about twenty a week to his savings. Avoids computer courses unless his boss asks.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, because hill sheep are hard for machines.
S1.quote: My father always said the man who shows up early is never the first to go. I hope he was right.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka's traditional values show in his answer: family and community before government. His deepest worry is succession on the farm, which he has prayed about. Working harder is his only strategy, and he half-admits it may not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three end at the same point, full AGI. They differ only in how much time there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies making these machines have run ahead of everyone, and somebody should have stopped them. I'd say churches and families need to look after their own. I'd not ask for handouts, but I'd not turn down help for others either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished. Two years, and I'm a junior shepherd with no other trade, getting married in a few months. I don't know how I'd stand in front of Grace's father and say I can provide for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Grace and cut the wedding back, chapel and a buffet at her parents' house, and keep the money as savings. I'd ask around chapel for any work, building, delivery, anything. If it got bad, we'd live with her parents for a while, and I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Ashamed, too, which I know doesn't make sense, because it wouldn't be my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man's meant to provide. That's how I was raised. I know robots aren't my fault, but my heart wouldn't care about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not ask for handouts. If it came to it, would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was that or Grace going without, yes. I'd hate it. I'd tell myself it's temporary, and I'd pay it back somehow, even if nobody asked me to.

S2.say: I'd say the companies making these machines ran ahead of everyone and should have been stopped, and churches and families need to look after their own. I wouldn't ask for handouts myself.
S2.think: I'd be finished, a junior shepherd with no other trade, getting married within months. I don't know how I'd tell my fiancée's father I can provide for her.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding back to chapel and a buffet at his fiancée's parents' house and keeps the money as savings. Asks around chapel for any work and moves in with her parents if things get bad.
S2.feel: Frightened, and ashamed even though he knows it wouldn't be his fault.
S2.quote: I know robots aren't my fault, but my heart wouldn't care about that.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture collides with Emeka's wedding and his idea of being a provider, and shame came up unprompted. His public line rejects handouts, but in private he would take government help rather than see his fiancée go without. Chapel is his first place to look for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with five years to see it coming. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to stand on their own feet if they start now. Apprenticeships, families helping each other, that kind of thing. I'd say government should get out of the way of people trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably keep on as I am for a good while, because I'd still be getting married and settling in. I'm not good with change, and I'd hope Mr Whitlock's way of farming lasts out his time at least. But I'd know it's coming, and I'd feel it every time I opened the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have the wedding, smaller, and I'd put off buying a cottage, renting instead. I'd save harder, aim for six months of money. I'd wait and see what the bigger farms do before I changed anything, because I don't want to chase something that goes anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like waiting for a storm you can see coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Grace change anything about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about starting a family soon after the wedding. With five years like this, I think we'd still try, but I'd want to know where the money comes from. Grace would say God provides. I'd say, yes, but he likes you to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start changing things earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Whitlock sat me down and told me straight. I'd listen to him more than any news. He's never told me anything that wasn't true.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people to stand on their own feet if they start now, through apprenticeships and families helping each other, with government out of the way.
S3.think: I'd probably carry on as I am for a while because of the wedding and settling in, hoping my boss's way of farming lasts his time. I'd feel it coming every time I opened the gate.
S3.do: Holds a smaller wedding, rents instead of buying a cottage and saves toward six months of money. Waits to see what bigger farms do before changing anything.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a storm coming over the hill.
S3.quote: Grace would say God provides. I'd say, yes, but he likes you to have a plan.
S3.fieldNote: Emeka would trim his family plans but not cancel them, and his faith shapes how he talks about planning. He'd be moved by his boss's word far more than by news. His public line about standing on your own feet sits beside private hope that change waits for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives a young man time to learn a proper trade, and that's what people should do, learn from someone who knows. Not wait for the government. I'd say it to the lads at young farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel steadier. Mr Whitlock will likely have retired, so I'd need a plan anyway. Ten years is long enough to learn something with my hands from a real teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shepherding for a few more years, have the wedding as planned, and save. Then I'd ask Grace's father, who's a stonemason, to take me on as an apprentice, because old walls and old churches need mending and I can't see a robot on a chapel roof. I'd not rush it, though, I'd wait a few years to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robots can do stonework too, by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be wrong, and I'd have learned something good anyway. I'd rather spend ten years learning a real craft than ten years being afraid. And people might still want a man to mend their chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Grace's father take being asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd make me wait a month to answer, that's his way. Then he'd say yes, and work me twice as hard as his other lad to make sure I meant it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years gives a young man time to learn a proper trade from someone who knows, instead of waiting for the government. I'd say it to the young farmers' club.
S4.think: I'd feel steadier, since my boss will likely have retired by then and I'd need a plan anyway. Ten years is long enough to learn a hand trade from a real teacher.
S4.do: Keeps shepherding for a few more years, holds the wedding as planned and saves. Later asks his fiancée's father, a stonemason, to take him on as an apprentice, without rushing.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: I can't see a robot on a chapel roof.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Emeka's traditional values point to a clear path: an apprenticeship with his future father-in-law. He accepts he could be wrong about stonework lasting and says the learning would still be worth it. Even here, he would wait a few years before moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would land on top of the wedding and I'd have nothing to offer Grace. What would help is apprenticeships for young men like me, paid properly, with real tradesmen. And for the chapel and the village to have the means to look after people, not just a payment from somewhere far away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Mr Whitlock. Men like him carry knowledge that isn't written anywhere. If the machines come and he's gone, it's lost. I'd like someone to write it down before then.

headlineQuote: Men like him carry knowledge that isn't written anywhere.
portrait: Emeka Farah is a 27-year-old junior shepherd at Greyfield, learning from his 70-year-old employer Mr Whitlock in the old way, and still struggling to make the sheepdog listen to him. He is marrying Grace at his chapel next August and has about four months of savings plus a wedding fund. He has never used AI and trusts people who admit their mistakes over machines. Mild change leaves him calm and steady change uneasy, while AGI in two years makes him frightened and ashamed because it would land on his wedding and his sense of being a provider. With ten years he would follow his faith and values toward an apprenticeship in stonemasonry with Grace's father.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would land on top of his wedding and leave him unable to provide for Grace.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid apprenticeships with real tradesmen, and resources for the chapel and village to look after people locally rather than a distant payment.
